      About the tracker and its method

      China–Georgia Investment Tracker is a register of investment in Georgia by mainland Chinese, Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned foreign brands, built from the Georgian-language press. It extends the China–Turkey Investment Tracker, the China–Hungary Investment Tracker, the China–Kazakhstan Investment Tracker and the China–Azerbaijan Investment Tracker to Georgia, the Black Sea end of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (Middle Corridor), with the same unit (a project), the same evidence (one claim per article, quoted word for word and linked) and the same reading of outcomes, and it keeps the registry checks of Gürel, Selamet, Şahinli, Sen and Tuzcu (2026), Asian Perspective 50(2): 219–257. Compiled by Osman Demirbağ, Burak Gürel, Kadir Selamet. Data release 2026-10-31.

      Definitions used on the first screen

      The headline, the squares and the four further findings use these terms. Counts follow the settings chosen above the squares (currently ).

      Realised
      Operating, under construction or acquired, as last reported.
      Live promise
      Announced, agreed, in talks or rumoured, with a press report found within the last .
      Dormant promise
      No press report found for or more ( projects at 2 / 3 / 5 years). This is not a confirmed cancellation: rest on a single press report.
      Failed or exited
      A bid lost or not made (), a promise abandoned or put on hold (), or an exit after realisation, by closure or sale ().
      Promise phase
      First reported as interest, talks, a bid or a promise: of the investment projects. The promise-phase base counts only these; projects that entered the press already realised, such as completed acquisitions, have no promise phase on record.
      Chinese
      Includes Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned brands. Mainland firms alone: realised. Taiwanese firms are excluded.
      Not counted
      non-equity or contractor and finance items: kept in the register and the explorer, not counted as investment.

      How the register was built

      The register follows the Turkey tracker's design and the three search stages of the Hungary tracker, so that firms nobody named in advance and reports that name no firm are caught as well. Every step leaves a file in the project repository, and every number on this page is computed from those files.

      1. Stage 1, known firms. 115 Chinese, Hong Kong and Macau firms and Chinese-owned brands, plus 23 names found later, searched under 209 terms in the search pages of 4 Georgian sites and in the article addresses and headlines listed by the sitemaps of 6 more.
      2. Stage 2, every China-related investment story. 24 Georgian queries such as ჩინური კომპანია, ჩინელი ინვესტორი or ქართულ-ჩინური in the same site searches, and the sitemap articles whose addresses or headlines name China.
      3. Stage 3, registries and China's own list. The GLEIF register of legal entities (167 Georgian records), and the main Chinese investors named by China's Ministry of Commerce in its country guide for Georgia.
      4. Fetch. Pages downloaded at a polite rate, text extracted, and every sentence naming a seed firm or China next to investment vocabulary kept as a candidate.
      5. Curation. 10 curation passes turned the candidates into projects and claims, each claim with the verbatim Georgian sentence, an English translation and the link; a script rejected any quote not found word for word in the downloaded article.
      6. Feedback. Names found by the curators and in stage 2 went back into stage 1 and were searched in the same way.

      Sources

      Google News, the search behind the Hungarian register, holds few Georgian-language articles. Both search stages therefore query the sites' own search pages: Civil.ge (Civil Georgia, the news site of the UN Association of Georgia), Forbes Georgia, Publika and the business site Marketer.ge. Each matches words anywhere in an article's text. Business Media Georgia, the Public Broadcaster (1tv.ge), Rustavi 2, TV Pirveli and On.ge answer scripted requests with HTTP 403 behind a firewall; the search pages of Radio Tavisupleba (the Georgian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty) and Business Press News are disallowed in their robots.txt, which the pipeline respects; Interpressnews and Netgazeti run their search in the browser. Six sites whose articles and sitemaps are open are searched through their sitemaps instead: the words of every article address, a Latin transliteration of the Georgian headline, or the headline given in the sitemap are matched (Interpressnews from 2008, Commersant.ge with headlines, Business Press News from 2013, Palitra News from 2024 and Kviris Palitra from 2019, and Imedi's latest 5,000 articles; the last three list only their recent articles).

      The source list (config/sources.csv) names 24 sources: news agency (1): Interpressnews; national news (4): Civil.ge, Publika, Radio Tavisupleba, On.ge; business news (5): Forbes Georgia, Marketer.ge, Commersant.ge, Business Press News, Business Media Georgia; broadcasters (6): Palitra News, Imedi, Georgian Public Broadcaster, Rustavi 2, TV Pirveli, Mtavari; national weeklies (1): Kviris Palitra; independent outlets (1): Netgazeti; official sources (3): Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development, Invest in Georgia, National Statistics Office of Georgia; registries (2): National Agency of Public Registry, GLEIF; Chinese official sources (1): MOFCOM country guide. The agencies and business sites (Interpressnews, Commersant, Business Press News, Forbes Georgia) carry most announcements, agreements and openings; Civil.ge, Publika, Netgazeti and Radio Tavisupleba report more of the conflicts (labour, land, environment, debts, the Anaklia port dispute). Claims by type of outlet: news agency 231, business news 120, national news 39, other outlets 12, official sources 4, broadcasters 2, national weeklies 1. Most cited: Interpressnews (231), Commersant.ge (61), Forbes Georgia (32), Civil.ge (23), Business Press News (19), Publika (12), Marketer.ge (8), Radio Tavisupleba (4), Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development (4), JAMnews (3).

      Stage 1: known Chinese firms

      The seed list holds 115 firms in three groups: 13 reported present in Georgia (the firms named in the MOFCOM country guide and in the Georgian press), 59 present in Azerbaijan, Turkey, Central Asia or Russia and 43 global majors whose presence in Georgia was to be checked. 23 names were added after the first curation.

      Each name was searched in all 4 site searches, up to ten pages per term and site, and in the article addresses and headlines of the 6 sitemap indexes. The Georgian press writes Chinese firm names in Latin letters (Hualing, Huawei, CRBC) with the Georgian ending after a hyphen (Hualing-ის), or in Georgian letters (ჰუალინგი, ჰუავეი), and translates the names of state-owned groups (ჩინეთის რკინიგზის 23-ე ბიურო). Because the site searches match a name anywhere in an article, the headline and lead decide what is downloaded: for firms known in Georgia they must name the firm or carry investment or China vocabulary (a Yutong bus in a road accident is not a Yutong story), for the others the firm next to investment or Georgia vocabulary, or China next to investment vocabulary. Georgian place names alone do not count, as nearly every headline has one. Sitemap addresses and headlines are read the same way.

      Georgian attaches case endings to names. A Latin name takes them after a hyphen or the closing quotation mark (Hualing-ის, „Huawei“-ს) or, now and then, straight on; a Georgian name takes them straight on (ჰუალინგის, ჩინეთში). As the endings are written in Georgian letters, a Latin name is never matched inside a longer Latin word (Gree in Green), and Georgian names shorter than four letters need an exact match or a hyphenated ending.

      Stage 2: every China-related investment story

      Generic Georgian queries catch firms that were not on the list and reports that name no firm at all (“ჩინური კომპანია …”). 24 queries, up to thirty pages each in every site search, and a scan of the sitemap addresses and headlines for words naming China returned 12,129 results, of which 2,570 had China (or a seed firm) and investment vocabulary in the headline, lead or address and were downloaded. Of the downloaded stage-2 articles, 1,174 carry a China-and-investment sentence tied to a Georgian place.

      ჩინური კომპანიაჩინური კომპანიისჩინური კომპანიებიჩინელი ინვესტორიჩინელი ინვესტორებიჩინური ინვესტიციაჩინური ინვესტიციებიჩინური კაპიტალიჩინური ქარხანაჩინური საწარმოჩინელმა ინვესტორმაჩინეთის ინვესტიციებიჩინური ბანკიჩინური სესხიჩინური სამშენებლო კომპანიაჩინელი ბიზნესმენიქართულ-ჩინურიჩინურ კომპანიასთანჩინური კომპანიის მიერჰონგ-კონგის კომპანიაჩინური ელექტრომობილიჩინური მხარეჩინეთის სახალხო რესპუბლიკის კომპანიაჩინური ჯგუფი

      Stage 2 and the curators' feedback round added 40 projects that the seed list had not reached, and 76 general signals: investment totals, unnamed investors, delegations and policy reviews.

      Stage 3: registries and China's own list

      No country list in Georgia. In Turkey, the ministry's list of foreign-capital firms gives each firm's country, and the Asian Perspective article checked it against the trade-registry gazette and the central registry. Georgia publishes no such list: the National Agency of Public Registry answers one company at a time, and its extracts name the company's partners.

      GLEIF. The open register of legal entity identifiers holds only 167 Georgian entities (Hungary has more than 26,000): identifiers are needed mainly by banks and bond issuers. Screening their parents and names found no entity with a Chinese, Hong Kong or Macau parent or a Chinese firm's name. GLEIF is a floor here, much more than in Hungary.

      China's own list. China's Ministry of Commerce names, in its country guide for outward investors (对外投资合作国别（地区）指南·格鲁吉亚, 2026 edition), the main Chinese investors and contractors in Georgia and the zones of the Hualing group. Of its 10 names, 10 were on the seed list; 10 are now covered by projects in the register. According to the guide, Chinese firms signed 12 new construction and engineering contracts in Georgia in 2025, worth USD 197 million.

      What the statistics say. China's Ministry of Commerce puts China's direct investment stock in Georgia at USD 1.23 billion at the end of 2025, after a flow of USD 69.65 million in 2025. Georgia's statistics office, as cited in the same guide, records USD 1.69 billion of foreign direct investment inflows in 2025 and a stock of USD 26.39 billion; China is not among the five largest sources of 2025 (the United Kingdom, Turkey, Malta, the United States and Azerbaijan). Chinese contractors signed 12 new contracts worth USD 197 million in 2025, by the same guide. Neither figure shows Chinese capital held through third jurisdictions such as the Netherlands, Cyprus, Singapore or Luxembourg. This is why the register records holding routes where they are documented (3 projects; Singapore 2, Luxembourg 1).

      Downloading and reading the articles

      The pages were downloaded directly at a polite rate (one request every one and a half seconds per site, shared by all workers and by the search and download processes). 3,582 articles were downloaded: 1,452 from stage 1, 2,030 from stage 2 and 100 added by the curators; 3,578 came with their full text from 23 domains.

      The texts were split into 51,922 sentences. A sentence became a candidate when it named a seed firm or China (ჩინეთი, ჩინური, ჩინელი, ჰონგ-კონგი …) next to investment vocabulary (ინვესტიცია, ქარხანა, საწარმო, წილი, მილიარდი …): 11,366 sentences in 2,845 articles, 3,587 of them naming a seed firm. Each candidate carries a lifecycle tier from ordered Georgian keyword rules (failure, other, realisation, interest, promise).

      Curation: from articles to projects and claims

      A project is a firm, or an identifiable investor, tied to a site or a target in Georgia; separate sites, stakes and separately reported phases are separate projects. A claim is one article and one step: the Georgian sentence copied character for character, its English translation, the article link, the date, the outlet and the step's label. Reports of Chinese interest that cannot be tied to a firm or site are general signals.

      What was filtered out, and why

      1. At the search stage, results were kept for download only when the headline or lead carried the vocabulary described above: 18,527 of 22,988 results were set aside. Some search terms are also ordinary words or match by stem, so most of their results were set aside: Transsion / Oppo / Vivo / Honor / Realme (phones) (687 results, 55 kept), Li Auto / Leapmotor / Nio / Xpeng (557 results, 10 kept), FAW Group (Hongqi) (389 results, 9 kept), DJI (348 results, 14 kept).
      2. At the reading stage, only sentences with a firm or China term next to investment vocabulary became candidates (11,366 of 51,922 sentences).
      3. Not Chinese. Taiwanese firms are excluded, and so are Turkish, Russian, Azerbaijani, Iranian and Western firms named next to a Chinese one unless a Chinese firm takes part in the step.
      4. Not investment. Chinese brands assembled or sold under licence by Georgian firms, and their dealers, are non-equity presence unless Chinese equity is reported, and so are air, cargo and rail routes, licences, consortia, technology partnerships and memoranda without a Chinese stake; construction contracts (road and rail sections, tunnels, bridges), Chinese loans, export credit and credit lines are contractor or finance items. None of them is counted as investment.
      5. Searched, but nothing in Georgia. Names with the most candidate articles and no project:

      Coding choices to review

      • Sites, stakes and phases that the press reports separately are separate projects: Hualing's Tbilisi Sea New City, its Kutaisi Free Industrial Zone and its purchase of Basisbank are three projects.
      • Joint ventures with the state (Partnership Fund, Georgian Railway, Georgian Oil and Gas Corporation, Georgian State Electrosystem, the Anaklia port company) are investment when the Chinese side holds equity; the Georgian partner is recorded.
      • Free industrial zones: the Chinese investor or operator of a free industrial zone (Poti, Kutaisi, Tbilisi), and a company in such a zone with a Chinese owner, are counted, and the zone is recorded as state support.
      • Purchases abroad: a Chinese-owned foreign brand or a company bought abroad (Volvo Cars of Geely, Pirelli of ChemChina) counts when its Georgian unit is reported.
      • Licence assembly: Chinese brands assembled or sold under licence by Georgian firms, and their dealers, are non-equity presence for the Chinese brand unless Chinese equity is reported.
      • Loans and contracts (EPC contracts, road and rail sections, tunnels and bridges, loans of China Development Bank, Exim Bank of China or Bank of China, export credit, credit lines) are kept as contractor or finance items, not as investment; road sections that the Roads Department tenders with ADB, World Bank, EIB, AIIB or JICA money are contracts of the Chinese builder.
      • Origin not established for 0 projects whose owners are described only as Chinese investors.

      Stages, outcomes, figures and the map

      Stages and outcomes

      Each project carries the stage it reached as last reported: realised or under way, agreed or announced, interest, talks or a bid, rumour, failed, lost or exited, non-equity presence, and contractor or finance only. The site reads the stage together with the time since the last report, as the Turkey tracker does. Realised and failed follow the stage. Announced, agreed, in-talks or rumoured projects are live promises while a report falls inside the dormancy window and dormant promises once none has been found for that long (three years by default; two and five are offered). A dormant promise means that no evidence of progress was found, not that the project was cancelled. A non-equity arrangement or a contract or loan is never counted as investment, even when its stage records that it ended.

      Claims and lifecycle tiers

      Each claim has a lifecycle tier read from its event label with ordered rules: failure words first, then later references and denials as “other”, then realisation, commitment and interest; a won tender counts as a commitment. The first realisation-tier claim dates a realisation, the first failure-tier claim a failure, and the first claim's tier records how the press first found the project. The time-to-outcome chart estimates the cumulative incidence of realisation and failure for projects first reported as interest or a promise (Aalen–Johansen), treating projects still open at the release as censored.

      Reported figures

      47 projects report a headline figure. Each was read by hand and classed by what it measures: 19 contract finance, 17 pledge, 9 project cost, 2 invested. Only announced pledges are compared across outcomes (17 projects). Lari, yuan, euro and rouble figures are converted to US dollars at the World Bank's annual average rate of the year the figure was reported (the latest published year for later years), so that they sit on the Turkey tracker's scale. Figures are as announced and not verified.

      The map

      Regions are those named in the articles: Tbilisi, the autonomous republics of Adjara and Abkhazia, and the nine regions (mkhare). A project with sites in several regions is counted in each, and 39 projects with no reported region are listed under “No region reported”. Outlines: geoBoundaries (from OpenStreetMap, ODbL), in which South Ossetia is a unit of its own; it is divided here as in Georgia's division, the Akhalgori district to Mtskheta-Mtianeti and the rest to Shida Kartli (the new borders are approximate). Neighbouring countries from Eurostat GISCO and lakes from Natural Earth; Lambert conformal conic projection with standard parallels at 41.5°N and 43°N.

      The first screen and the explorer

      The headline, the squares and the four further findings describe all investment projects as last reported, on the comparison base and dormancy threshold chosen there; explorer filters do not change them, they highlight the matching projects. Outcome, sector, origin and form filters are inclusive within a group and combine across groups. A link to any view can be copied from the results bar, and each project opens its evidence timeline with the Georgian quotes, their translations and links to the articles.

      Limits

      This is a register of press reports, not of capital flows. A promise can be realised without the press noticing, and a realised project may have had a promise phase no archive captured. The archives reach back unevenly: of the sitemaps, Interpressnews's start in 2008, Business Press News's in 2013, Kviris Palitra's in 2019 and Palitra News's in 2024, and Imedi's list only its latest 5,000 articles. Business Media Georgia, the Public Broadcaster, Rustavi 2, TV Pirveli and On.ge could not be read and Netgazeti and Radio Tavisupleba could not be searched, so their reports enter the register only as carried by other outlets or found otherwise; Russian- and English-language reports are quoted only where no Georgian report of a step was found. The National Agency of Public Registry answers one company at a time, so the owners and stakes of Georgian companies rest on its extracts where checked, on press reports, company disclosures and GLEIF; the evidence for each attribution is named in the curation notes of the project. Recent cohorts are right-censored, and some associations are built into the data: holding routes are documented mostly once a company exists, and a named region is itself a sign of progress. Treat such differences as descriptive.
